name: Information Society (InfoSoc) Directive
evidence_rating: thin: Commission-commissioned legal evaluation and later IA diagnosis; no causal study of the Directive itself; indirect causal evidence on DRM and correlational evidence on research exceptions
summary: The InfoSoc Directive promised to harmonise copyright across the EU and spur online content services, but set no measurable targets. The Commission's own 2007 evaluation found it harmonised copyright exceptions only 'very modestly' and created legal uncertainty around copy protection (DRM), and in 2016 the Commission proposed new mandatory exceptions to fix the same problems. Independent research suggests restrictive exceptions are linked to less data-mining research and that removing DRM raised music sales by about 10%, but no study measures the Directive's overall economic effect.

indicators.objective: The 1997 proposal (COM(97) 628) predates the Commission's impact assessment and financial-statement indicator system; it set no measurable targets. Monitoring relied on the Article 12 review clause

indicators.indicator: Reduce legal fragmentation across Member States so that online content services can operate cross-border
indicators.evidence: Commission-commissioned study (IViR 2007) found the harmonising effect of the optional list of exceptions 'very modest at best', producing a 'mosaic' of national rules; the Commission's own 2007 review confirmed very diverse national provisions. The 2016 copyright impact assessment again cited legal uncertainty over exceptions (teaching, text and data mining, preservation) as a major problem, leading to new mandatory exceptions in Directive 2019/790.

indicators.objective: Growth and innovation in online content services
indicators.indicator: Foster investment in creativity and new online business models
indicators.evidence: Never measured quantitatively. The IViR evaluation concluded the Directive had 'at best only partly achieved' its goal of promoting growth and innovation in online content services. No causal study isolates the Directive's effect on creative output or investment.

indicators.indicator: Legal protection of DRM to support new digital distribution models while safeguarding exceptions (Art. 6(4))
indicators.evidence: IViR found the DRM rules created 'confusion, legal uncertainty and disharmonisation'; Member States chose widely different mechanisms to safeguard exceptions. Independent evidence from the music industry (Zhang 2018) shows that dropping DRM raised digital sales by about 10%, suggesting DRM did not support sales as assumed.

indicators.indicator: Exceptions allow scientific research uses without hampering innovation
indicators.evidence: Cross-country bibliometric evidence links copyright regimes that require rightholder consent for data mining (as in most EU states under the InfoSoc list) to a markedly smaller share of data-mining research output (Handke et al. 2015).

literature.citation: Westkamp, Rieber-Mohn, van Eechoud, Guibault, Helberger & Hugenholtz (IViR) (2007), Study on the Implementation and Effect in Member States' Laws of Directive 2001/29/EC, Study for the European Commission (DG Internal Market)
literature.authors: Westkamp, Rieber-Mohn, van Eechoud, Guibault, Helberger & Hugenholtz (IViR)
literature.title: Study on the Implementation and Effect in Member States' Laws of Directive 2001/29/EC
literature.venue: Study for the European Commission (DG Internal Market)
literature.outcomes: harmonisation; legal certainty; online business models
literature.headline: Harmonising effect of the optional exceptions 'very modest at best', a 'mosaic' of national rules; DRM rules offer 'confusion, legal uncertainty and disharmonisation'; the Directive 'at best only partly achieved' its goal of promoting growth and innovation in online content services
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's own commissioned evaluation found the Directive did little to harmonise copyright exceptions across the EU and only partly met its goal of boosting online content services.
literature.quality: legal analysis; no quantitative impact estimates

literature.citation: European Commission (2007), Report to the Council, the European Parliament and the Economic and Social Committee on the application of Directive 2001/29/EC, SEC(2007) 1556 (summary via European Parliament Legislative Observatory)
literature.title: Report to the Council, the European Parliament and the Economic and Social Committee on the application of Directive 2001/29/EC
literature.venue: SEC(2007) 1556 (summary via European Parliament Legislative Observatory)
literature.method: review of transposition and national case law (Arts 5, 6, 8)
literature.headline: Courts often sidestepped the exceptions by interpreting the reproduction right; national private-copying, library and parody exceptions very diverse; Member States chose very different mechanisms (none, mediation, courts, administrative bodies) to reconcile DRM with exceptions
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's first review found Member States had implemented the copyright exceptions and anti-circumvention rules in very different ways.
literature.quality: legal review only; no economic data

literature.citation: European Commission (2016), Impact assessment on the modernisation of EU copyright rules (executive summary SWD(2016) 302), SWD(2016) 301
literature.title: Impact assessment on the modernisation of EU copyright rules (executive summary SWD(2016) 302)
literature.method: ex-ante (for successor Directive 2019/790); includes problem review of InfoSoc exceptions
literature.outcomes: legal certainty; research; education; cultural heritage
literature.headline: Legal uncertainty over acts allowed under existing exceptions in the digital environment identified as a major issue for teachers, researchers doing text and data mining, and cultural heritage institutions; new mandatory exceptions proposed
literature.summary_plain: Fifteen years on, the Commission concluded that the Directive's optional exceptions left teachers, researchers and libraries uncertain about what they may do online, and proposed new mandatory exceptions.

literature.citation: Handke, Guibault & Vallbe (2015), Is Europe Falling Behind in Data Mining? Copyright's Impact on Data Mining in Academic Research, ELPUB 2015 proceedings, IOS Press (SSRN 2608513)
literature.title: Is Europe Falling Behind in Data Mining? Copyright's Impact on Data Mining in Academic Research
literature.method: cross-country panel regression (bibliometric data, 42 countries, 1992-2014); correlational
literature.headline: Where data mining requires express rightholder consent, it accounts for a significantly smaller share of research output; authors describe it as the first empirical study to find a significant negative association between copyright protection and innovation
literature.summary_plain: Countries whose copyright law requires permission for text and data mining - including most EU states before 2019 - produce noticeably less data-mining research.
literature.quality: observational; not a strict causal design

literature.citation: Zhang (2018), Intellectual Property Strategy and the Long Tail: Evidence from the Recorded Music Industry, Management Science 64(1), 24-42
literature.title: Intellectual Property Strategy and the Long Tail: Evidence from the Recorded Music Industry
literature.method: causal: difference-in-differences (DRM removal by major labels, ~5,900 albums)
literature.headline: Removing DRM increased digital album sales by about 10%, with large gains for lower-selling ('long tail') albums and no benefit for top sellers
literature.summary_plain: When record labels dropped copy protection (DRM), digital music sales rose about 10%, mostly for lesser-known albums - evidence that the DRM the Directive protects did not help sales.
literature.quality: not EU-specific; tests DRM, not the Directive itself
